title: Dabur — Risk & Reputation Research
content:
According to reviews on PissedConsumer, Dabur has a 1.8 star rating from 19 customer reviews, indicating mostly dissatisfied consumers. Common complaints include refund requests, delivery failures, damaged or poor quality products, and allegations of fraud and unresponsive customer service. On ConsumerComplaints.in, complaints highlight issues such as bad quality juice, honey turning into sugar crystals, and finding foreign objects like cotton buds, worms, and metal taars in products. Positive feedback mentions affordability and specific products like air oil.

According to reviews on PissedConsumer, there are frequent complaints about non-delivery, delayed or missing refunds, damaged, expired, or poor quality items, and alleged fraudulent online listings. Additionally, there are reports of poor customer service responsiveness and dispute resolution. On the other hand, IJERT's case study mentions delivery delays, incomplete orders, and stock gaps, as well as issues with complaint resolution and expired or damaged product handling. The FDA has also taken action against Dabur India for systemic data-integrity and cGMP failures, highlighting broader failures in quality culture, data integrity, and manufacturing control.

The FDA said the deficiencies went beyond isolated documentation errors, describing them as evidence of a “systemic breakdown” in quality unit (QU) oversight and a deficient quality culture.FDA escalates action against Dabur India over systemic data-integrity and cGMP failures [...] The regulatory agency said Dabur's response to the Form 483 did not adequately address the deficiencies, noting that the problems it identified reflected broader failures in quality culture, data integrity and manufacturing control.

## "Systemic" data-integrity failures [...] The US FDA has issued a Warning Letter to Indian OTC medication manufacturer Dabur, following an FDA inspection of the firm's OTC drug manufacturing facility in Dadra and Nagar Haveli, India.

The letter follows a Form 483, made public in May of this year, in which the FDA detailed deliberate falsification of equipment usage logs, no cleaning validation and a live bird in the raw material warehouse after the inspection in January.

Dabur India Limited is involved in multiple legal disputes. One notable case is the lawsuit against YouTuber Dhruv Rathee, which was settled on June 18 after nearly a year of litigation. Another significant case is against Patanjali, co-founded by Baba Ramdev, over misleading claims in an advertisement for chyawanprash, being heard in the Delhi High Court. Additionally, Dabur has been involved in various other litigations including a case against Colgate over ad claims, a trademark dispute with Emami, and a case against Patanjali over an ad deemed denigrating.

After nearly a year of litigation, a dispute between Dabur India Limited ('Dabur') and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee reached a resolution on June 18. Dabur had filed a lawsuit to protect its intellectual property rights against a YouTube video by Dhruv Rathee referencing 'Real', one of Dabur's products. The case was settled before a Single Judge Bench presided over by Justice Krishna Rao, who approved an agreement between the parties. The settlement included the removal of all 'Real' trademarks, [...] The Court tried to balance the intention of an individual and the power of multinational companies; in a previous hearing dated April 03, 2023, the Calcutta High Court expressed dissatisfaction with Dabur India’s efforts to remove all URLs of a video by YouTuber Dhruv Rathee concerning Real fruit juice. Justice Ravi Krishan Kapur emphasised to Dabur that the Court would require evidence of Rathee's malicious intent before issuing such an order. This underscores the Court's impartiality, [...] By an order dated February 29, 2024, the Court suggested that the parties resolve the disputes in the suit by blurring or removing fruit juice packets alleged to resemble Dabur's products. In response, Dhruv Rathee proposed via email on March 15, 2024, to blur or use generic fruit juice packaging, asserting his rights to freedom of speech, expression, and fair comment. Dabur accepted this proposal in principle, as conveyed in their email dated March 19, 2024. Subsequently, Dhruv Rathee

Dabur filed a lawsuit against Patanjali, co-founded by Baba Ramdev, over claims made in an advertisement for chyawanprash. Dabur alleges that the ad includes misleading statements about the herbs used and product safety. The case is being heard in the Delhi High Court. The dispute highlights the ongoing rivalry between the two major Ayurvedic product brands.

According to PissedConsumer, Dabur D2C operations have faced significant reputation problems and criticism, including frequent customer complaints about non-delivery, delayed or missing refunds, damaged, expired, or poor quality items, and alleged fraudulent online listings. The company has also been reported for poor customer service responsiveness and dispute resolution, with a 1.8 star rating from 19 customer reviews indicating mostly dissatisfied consumers. However, WARC mentions that Dabur has shifted its focus from revenue operations to brand building and acquiring first-party data in its D2C efforts. The sources do not provide a definitive answer to the overall success or failure of Dabur's D2C strategy.

- Frequent customer complaints about non delivery and delayed or missing refunds.
- Multiple reports of damaged, expired, or poor quality items and alleged fraudulent online listings.
- Poor customer service responsiveness and dispute resolution.

Positive Feedback

Some reviewers note affordability and specific products like air oil as pros.

Key Takeaways for Future Customers [...] I had ordered vide order no 341018 three bottles of mustard oil. I just received them and when i opened the bottles were leaking and no gift item was in the box .

Why it matters

The economics of D2C defeated Ask Dabur, the company’s previous effort in this area which was “a complete bleed”, CEO Mohit Malhotra told an earnings call. This time, however, the emphasis has shifted away from a revenue operation and towards brand building and acquiring first-party data.

Takeaways

- Well-known trademark protection – ‘Dabur’ is a well-known trademark, enjoying the highest level of protection. Misuse in domain names was inherently deceptive and not a case of descriptive use or coincidence.
- Impersonation versus confusion – the court distinguished between mere confusion and complete impersonation. The defendants were not just creating uncertainty but were posing as Dabur itself, which undermines consumer trust in online transactions. [...] - Dishonest adoption – the defendants used the mark ‘Dabur’ in domain names with words such as “franchise” and “distributor”, creating a misleading impression of authenticity. Fraudulent domain names were used to host websites impersonating Dabur, displaying its logos and product images, and soliciting payments under the guise of offering distributorships and franchise opportunities. These acts amounted to complete impersonation, deceiving consumers and causing significant financial losses. [...] The internet has transformed how businesses reach consumers, but it has also quietly created new avenues for deception. What once required physical imitation through fake labels, counterfeit goods, or misleading shopfronts can now be achieved with a single domain name and a convincing website. The High Court of Delhi’s judgment in Dabur India v Ashok Kumar & Ors, delivered on December 24 2025, is a response to this evolving reality.
